metadata.title: Groundwater: The Wells That Keep Dropping
metadata.section: Section E: Energy, Climate & Natural Resources
metadata.visual_form: Three wells: water level vs. the early 1980s
metadata.data_notes: Each well is compared with its own 1980-1985 level, then averaged across all long-record USGS wells in the zone. Above zero = the water table is lower than in the early 1980s. Wells are measured about once a year. No usable long-record USGS wells exist in California's Central Valley (that data is kept by the state).

series_manifest.label: High Plains South: Kansas, Oklahoma, Texas (13 wells)
High Plains North: Nebraska and North (1863 wells)
Floridan Aquifer: Florida and Georgia (56 wells)

events.label: Florida drought: Floridan level drops 5 feet
Southern High Plains falls 4 feet in one year
Plains drought: heavy pumping for irrigation
Southern High Plains 21 feet below 1980s level

explanation.summary: Farms and cities pump water from underground layers of rock and sand called aquifers. This chart shows how far the water level in wells has dropped since the early 1980s. In the southern High Plains (Kansas, Oklahoma, Texas), it keeps falling year after year. In Nebraska and in Florida, it goes up and down with the weather and has changed far less.
explanation.methodology: Depth-to-water field measurements (USGS parameter 72019) from the USGS Water Data API, for wells measured from before 1981 to recent years. Each well is compared with its own 1980-1985 average, then wells are averaged. The High Plains (Ogallala) aquifer is split at the Kansas-Nebraska border (40°N). Most southern High Plains wells are measured by state agencies, so only 13 long-record USGS wells qualify there. California's Central Valley has no usable long-record USGS wells, so it is not shown.

key_findings.title: 2000: The Slow Decline
key_findings.description: By 2000 the water in the southern High Plains wells was 6.2 feet lower than in the early 1980s, falling about a third of a foot every year.
key_findings.significance: Irrigation pumps take out more water than rain puts back.

key_findings.title: 2008: A Big Drop
key_findings.description: The southern level fell 4 feet in a single year, from 11.5 to 15.5 feet below its early-1980s level, during a dry period with heavy pumping.
key_findings.significance: Droughts speed up the decline because farmers pump more.

key_findings.title: 2024: 21 Feet Lower
key_findings.description: The southern High Plains wells are 20.6 feet lower than in the early 1980s. In Nebraska (1,863 wells) it is 2.6 feet lower, and in the Floridan aquifer it is about the same as in the early 1980s.
key_findings.significance: The aquifer under the southern Plains is being used up much faster than the northern part.
